title: They Lived to See the Promise
lead: Those who waited their whole lives saw the day come. God does not forget a person who prays for the same thing for years.
questions: What have I been praying about the longest, and am I ready to keep waiting with God, like Simeon, without setting Him a deadline?
Has my knowledge of Scripture and of church matters taken the place of a waiting heart, and how would I know?
Which of the long-waiting, prayer-soaked people in my community should I ask what they see before I plan the future?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Forty days after the night in Bethlehem, there are no more angels and no more shepherds. Mary and Joseph bring the Child to the temple and offer “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons,” the sacrifice provided for families who cannot afford a lamb. The Son of God began life in a family that paid the rate for the poor. And yet in the crowd two people are waiting who will recognize in a forty-day-old baby what no one else in the whole building noticed.

Simeon “was waiting for the consolation of Israel,” and he had been given a promise the size of one lifetime: he would not die until he had seen the Messiah. In three sentences Luke mentions the Holy Spirit three times: the Spirit was upon him, the Spirit revealed it to him, and led by the Spirit he came, at the very moment “when the parents brought in the child Jesus.” A man who had let himself be led through years of waiting also let himself be brought to the one right minute. He takes the Baby in his arms and says: “Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace. For my eyes have seen Your salvation.” He did not see the end of the story, only its beginning, and that was enough for him. And his song holds the moment we have been waiting for: this salvation is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles.” In a temple whose inner courts were closed to Gentiles, the most faithful of Israelites announces that the Child is for them too. The closer to God, the more room for outsiders.

Anna is there too: a prophetess, widowed after seven years of marriage, who for decades had not left the temple. She is the daughter of Phanuel, whose name means “face of God,” and she belongs to the tribe of Asher, which history had long since written off as lost. With God, neither tribes nor people get lost. It is she, a widow in her eighties, who “spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem”: the first evangelist, before any of the Twelve had so much as learned to walk. In this scene God was recognized not by the priests or the experts in regulations, but by two old people whose only qualification was waiting with the Spirit. Knowing the letter cannot replace a waiting heart.

Yesterday the army of heaven sang over the fields of Bethlehem and the shepherds ran to the manger. Forty days later there is no trace left of that night. The angels have gone, the shepherds are back with their sheep, and Mary and Joseph are doing what every poor family in Israel did after a son was born: going to the temple to take care of the formalities the Law required. No one gives them a second glance. Hundreds of families just like them, with babies in their arms, pass through the courts. And in this ordinary, official scene two people are waiting who will recognize in a forty-day-old Child what no one else in the whole building noticed. The section we are walking through is addressed to those who have waited their whole lives. Today we meet two such people by name.

sections.heading: The Offering of the Poor
paragraphs: Luke notes that the parents brought “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” That detail says more than it seems to. After a birth the Law called for the offering of a lamb, but a family that could not afford a lamb was allowed to bring two birds. Jesus’ parents used the rate for the poor. The Son of God began life in a family that had to be excused from paying the full price. And behind this humblest of offerings, interestingly, stood a whole infrastructure: all across Judea archaeologists are digging up columbaria, underground pigeon farms with thousands of nesting niches carved into the rock. In one such cave, hidden in a pot, they even found Tyrian shekels, the currency of the temple tax. Breeding, transport, currency: the offering of the poor was an ordinary branch of the economy. Poverty in Israel was not an embarrassing exception that no one had written a procedure for. It was everyday life, and the Law had a separate, fully valid provision for it.

It is also worth reading carefully why this offering was made at all. The regulation speaks of the mother’s purification after childbirth, but in the whole chapter of the Law that deals with it there is no mention of any wrongdoing, any guilt, or any forgiveness. Impurity after childbirth was ritual, not moral: it came from the natural, unavoidable course of life, and it was nobody’s offense. Mary is not bringing the birds to make up for some wrong. She brings them because this is how the time after a child’s birth is brought to a close. That distinction is one we still need today: not everything that keeps a person out of the community for a while is their fault. Israel’s Law knew how to tell the difference. We don’t always.

sections.heading: A Man Who Knew How to Wait
paragraphs: Then Simeon steps onto the scene. Luke sketches him in three strokes: righteous, devout, and “waiting for the consolation of Israel.” That last phrase matters most. Behind the word “consolation” stands the Greek paraklesis, and Israel knew it from the prophet: “Comfort, comfort My people,” says your God (Isaiah 40:1). The consolation of Israel was not a pleasant mood but a concrete hope: that God would come and take up His people’s cause. From this same root John would later form a name for the Holy Spirit: the Paraclete, the Comforter. So Simeon was waiting for what the whole Bible is waiting for.

And he was given a promise cut to the measure of one life: “he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.” Notice how densely Luke writes about the Holy Spirit here. The Spirit was upon Simeon, the Spirit revealed the promise to him, and led by the Spirit he came into the temple. Three sentences, the Spirit three times. And the fourth sentence is about timing: he came in just as “the parents brought in the child Jesus.” Not an hour earlier and not a day later. A man who had let himself be led through years of waiting also let himself be brought to the one right minute. The punctuality of this scene is not to Simeon’s credit; it is to the credit of the faithfulness of the One who had promised.

sections.heading: Now
paragraphs: Simeon takes the Baby in his arms and begins with the word his whole life had been working toward: “Now you are releasing your servant, Master, according to your word, in peace” (WEB). That is what a watchman hears when he is relieved after a long watch: your duty is done, you may go. But the most astonishing part is the reason he gives: “for my eyes have seen your salvation” (WEB). What exactly had those eyes seen? A forty-day-old baby of poor parents. No miracle, no throne, none of the things that were still to come. Simeon did not see the end of the story. He saw its beginning, and that was enough for him to die in peace. There is a lesson here about the nature of hope: it doesn’t need to see everything. It needs to see enough to know whose hands hold the rest. And one more thing: in this sentence salvation is not a concept or a doctrine. It lies in an old man’s arms, it breathes, and it has to be held carefully. Ever since God came in the flesh, salvation has had a face.

sections.heading: A Light That Belongs to No One
paragraphs: In Simeon’s next words something happens that we have been waiting for in this series for a long time. He speaks of the salvation “which You have prepared in the sight of all people, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel.” All people. The Gentiles. In a temple whose inner courts were closed to Gentiles, an old Israelite announces that this Child is for them too. Simeon did not invent this thought; he took it from the songs about the Servant of the Lord, who was to be a light for the nations. That had been Israel’s role from the start: a people chosen so that the light would travel onward, through them to everyone. History has shown how easily the calling “a light for others” turns into “a light for us.” Simeon, a man of the deepest tradition, of prayer and of the Law, is living proof that faithfulness to your own heritage and a wide heart for outsiders do not merely coexist; they belong together. The closer he was to the God of Israel, the more room he saw for those outside Israel.

sections.heading: A Sword in the Blessing
paragraphs: Simeon blesses the family, but he does not wrap hope in cotton wool. He tells Mary hard things: this Child will be a sign that is spoken against; because of Him many will fall and many will rise; “and a sword will pierce your soul as well.” A single speech holds both the light of the nations and a sword in a mother’s heart. This is an important feature of biblical hope: it does not rest on a promise that nothing will hurt. Simeon sees that around this Child “the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed,” that no one will be able to stay neutral about Him. A real encounter with God does not leave a person the way it found them: it lifts some up, lays others bare, and sometimes does both at once. Whoever promises people a faith that costs nothing is describing a different faith from the one Simeon held in his arms that day.

sections.heading: Anna Had Been There All Along
paragraphs: There is one more person in this scene. Luke writes: “There was also a prophetess named Anna.” Simeon came to the temple that day; Anna was simply there. “She never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying.” Her life story fits into two numbers: seven years of marriage, and eighty-four, which may be the years of her widowhood or her age. Either way, decades of loneliness prayed through in one place. Luke adds two details that are easy to miss. Anna is the daughter of Phanuel, and that name means “face of God.” In the form Penuel it was the name of the place by the Jabbok where Jacob, as we remember from day seven of our journey, saw God face to face. The daughter of “God’s face” lived to see the day when she looked God in the face quite literally. And the second detail: Anna comes from the tribe of Asher, one of the northern tribes carried off by Assyria seven centuries earlier and counted by history as lost. History wrote them off, but God evidently kept His books more carefully: on the day the Messiah appears in the temple, a daughter of a “lost” tribe is there too. With God, neither tribes nor individual people get lost.

And it is Anna, a woman, a widow, someone whose voice counted for little in that culture, who becomes the first person in this Gospel to tell others publicly about Jesus: she “spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.” The shepherds spoke about what had been announced to them; Anna speaks about Someone she has seen. An aged widow became the first evangelist before any of the Twelve had so much as learned to walk.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: Finally, notice who recognized God in this scene. Not the priest on duty, though he had the regulations for every offering at his fingertips. Not the scholars of Scripture, though they could point to Bethlehem with their eyes closed. He was recognized by two old people whose only qualification was that they waited with the Spirit and did not stop. That is a question for us too, people who are often very well versed in the letter: knowing the regulations cannot replace a waiting heart. You can take care of God’s business and miss the God who is walking across the courtyard right now.

And if you have been praying about the same thing for years and nothing changes, this story is for you. Simeon and Anna waited longer than most of us live. God did not lose their case or mix up the dates; He came at the right moment, just as He had promised. Your long waiting is not proof that He has forgotten you. Sometimes it is the place where He is preparing your eyes for what He wants to show you. And one more thing, for us as a community: the Simeons and Annas are sitting in our pews. People who have prayed through decades sometimes see further than all our committees put together. Before we plan the future, it is worth asking those who have waited the longest what they see.
